Chapter 6: The Art of Asking Better Questions
You know, sometimes the real difference between feeling stuck and actually moving forward is as simple as the questions we ask ourselves.
It's surprising how much our inner dialogue shapes what we experience day to day. If you let your mind run on autopilot, it can just loop through the same old worries or assumptions—never really breaking out of that rut.
But here's the thing: when you learn to ask better questions—questions that are more open, more curious, and way less judgmental—suddenly, you start to see new paths you hadn't noticed before. Doors begin to open.
Let me share a story with you.
There was this manager who always felt overwhelmed by team conflicts. The question running through their head was, “Why can’t they just get along?” But honestly, that question didn’t help at all. It just led to more frustration.
Then, after one especially tense meeting, a different question popped up: “What might each person be needing right now?” That tiny shift changed everything.
Instead of feeling frustrated, the manager started to feel empathy. They began listening more closely, actually asking team members what would help them feel supported. And you know what? The atmosphere started to warm up. People relaxed. Solutions began to appear—solutions no one had seen before.
The truth is, most of us don’t even realize how often our questions are just hidden judgments. Think about it—questions like, “Why am I always behind?” or “What’s wrong with me?” They don’t really move us forward, do they?
But if you switch it up and ask, “What’s one small thing I could try differently?” or “Who could I ask for help?”—well, suddenly your mind starts looking for possibilities, not just problems.
There’s another story that comes to mind. A student was constantly struggling with self-doubt, always haunted by the question, “Am I good enough?” One day, a mentor suggested a new question: “What am I learning from this?”
That change in focus—moving from trying to prove their worth to simply growing—was like letting out a breath they didn’t know they were holding. The pressure eased. The student took more risks, tried new things, and started seeing mistakes as just part of the process.
So, asking better questions isn’t about having all the answers. It’s about being willing to look at things from a different angle—to challenge your assumptions, and to invite a little curiosity into the mix.
Most of us fall into the habit of asking questions that keep us stuck. But with a bit of practice, you can actually teach your mind to become your ally—helping you move forward, discover possibilities, and grow beyond what you thought was possible.
